entries.note: The Romans' language is called Latin because it was the language of the Latins, people of the region Latium.
Ancient region around Rome and the lower Tiber; modern Italians call it Lazio, also a football team's name.
From Old French, late Latin 'in the Roman manner'; used for Latin-descended languages and later for novels.
Borrowed from the Romans by Germanic dialects on the continent, before English existed as a language.
Another Latin loan picked up from the Romans before the Germanic dialects reached Britain.
From Latin for a thousand paces, since a Roman mile was a thousand paces long.
Early Latin borrowing, originally about battle; related to German Kampf, campaign and champion.
From Latin strata, as in via strata, so saying street is essentially saying 'straight'.
From Latin vallum; the hosts note classical Latin pronounced V as W.
From Latin castellum, entering late Old English often through biblical usage; later borrowed again as chateau.
A later French borrowing of the same Latin word that gave castle.
Arrived with Christian missionaries; probably from adolere 'to burn' rather than altus 'high'.
Latin word for a chest, then a chest holding relics, then a venerated place.
Probably came through other Germanic languages first, ultimately from Latin pulvinus, a small cushion.
Latin for road or path, hidden inside many English words; one of Jess's favourite roots.
One of the words Jess used to teach fifth graders the Latin root meaning 'to speak'.
Shares the 'speak' root; Jess's students guessed its meaning from eloquent and soliloquy.
Another word from the Latin root meaning to talk or speak, used in Jess's class.
Grand plus the 'speak' root, so literally big talking; William Barnes suggested 'high talking' instead.
Sleep-talking; students worked it out through the link with insomnia.
Literally in the way or in front of you on the road, so easy to trip over.
Im- 'not', per 'through', via 'road'; resistant to attack because there is no way through.
From via; something that happens earlier on your route or path.
From via; to stray away from the course.
Along with deviant, means straying from the moral path; from via.
Came through French from Latin viaticum, a journey, which contains via.
From via; to carry something with you along a road.
From via; someone sent somewhere to represent another person.
Related to envoy; asks for a payment to be sent along. There's no voice in it, only a road.
A place where three roads met and people traded news; the fun-fact sense came from Logan Pearsall Smith's 1902 books.
Suggests the unimportant street talk of commoners gathered at Roman crossroads.
The three classical arts of grammar, logic and rhetoric, named during the Carolingian Renaissance.
The four advanced subjects (arithmetic, astronomy, music, geometry) studied after the trivium; the older term.
Jess packs fourteen related words into one riff, including depend, pendulum, suspense and compensate.
From pensare, a frequentative of pendere; something hanging on your mind.
From Latin ponderare 'to weigh', linked to pendere; spelled roughly as a French speaker might say it.
From libra pondo, where pondo means weight; tied to the same weighing and hanging family.
Root in maintain, abstain, entertain, obtain and detain, all basically meaning to hold.
Literally to hold in the hand, an example of how literal Latin compounds really are.
Renaissance backlash against classical borrowings; the name may come from dipping into the inkhorn often for long words.
Sir John Cheke used this instead of centurion in his Gospel of Matthew without loanwords.
Cheke's native substitute for crucified; the hosts think it sounds like a euphemism.
Cheke's term, perhaps for exodus or diaspora; the hosts point out it isn't any shorter.
William Barnes's Germanic replacement for astronomy.
William Barnes's Germanic replacement for ornithology.
First assumed to replace knowledge, but it was proposed for logic; reason and idea were French anyway.
Sub plus a verb of looking: an example of the prefix sub assimilating to the following sound.
Sub plus a verb meaning to come after, with the b assimilated to c.
Sub plus ferre 'to carry', so literally to be under a burden; assimilated prefix.
Latin prefix meaning not or away, as in distribute; French de-/des- words use the same prefix.
From Latin oblivio, forgetfulness; sending something into a state of empty nothingness.
Ob- plus litera 'letter'; originally to erase or blot out writing.
Toward noxa, hurt or injury; the Latin meant injurious, much stronger than today's 'annoying'.
The initial o- is really ob-, another example of assimilation.
Ob- 'in front of' plus fuscare 'to make something dark'.
Ob- plus a Latin element the hosts say means covered, also seen in chiaroscuro.
Art term meaning bright-dark, sharing the obscure element; earlier covered in their art episode.
A little-known ob- word meaning to walk around.
Means sleepwalking; Rob was reaching for it after obambulation.
Latin suffix freely added to Germanic stems like watchable, winnable and knowable, making hybrid words.
A hybrid of Latin inter and Greek planet.
An 18th-century non-hybrid alternative, with mundane meaning worldly.
Octopi is wrong in Latin and octopodes isn't really Greek, so octopuses is safest.
Like prospectus and status, its Latin plural is unchanged, not -i; some people still use apparatus as the plural.
Latin for body; the plural is corpora, not corpi.
Latin for hand; the plural is manus too, not mani.
Plural of alga; there's no English plural like algas, and algae is often used as singular.
A Latin plural used as a singular; from agere 'to do', once paired theologically with credenda.
Theological counterpart to agenda: things to be believed versus things to be done.
Shares a root with act and actor; both are 'doers', one on stage and one on someone's behalf.
Latin for doorkeeper or porter, related to Janus; became a school usher, then a caretaker by the 1700s.
Two-faced Roman god of doorways, linked to janitor; January is named after him.
Originally a sandy place, since amphitheatres were strewn with sand; the deeper root may be Etruscan.
From the two unlucky 'Egyptian days' marked each month; first used as the noun phrase 'in the dismal'.
Roman calendar lists of days allowed for official business; Jess enjoys the pun 'the fasti of Furius'.
Originally meant lasting one day, from dies; a doublet with journal.
The word diurnal squashed through French; a doublet of diary.
Originally meant noon; Latin medidies became meridies by dissimilation, D changing to R.
